questions.prompt: Sort each change on Earth's surface into the process it shows.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort six changes into three processes: weathering, erosion, or deposition. The changes are: rainwater reacts with minerals in a boulder and its surface slowly crumbles; a tree root widens a crack in a boulder; wind lifts loose sand off a dune and carries it away; gravity pulls loose rock and soil down a steep slope; a river slows as it enters a lake and drops its sand; and a melting glacier leaves behind a ridge of the rock it carried.

items.text: Rainwater reacts with minerals in a boulder, and its surface slowly crumbles
items.rationale: Weathering: a chemical reaction is breaking the rock down right where it sits.

items.text: A tree root widens a crack in a boulder
items.rationale: Weathering: living things can break rock down too, and the pieces stay in place.

items.text: Wind lifts loose sand off a dune and carries it away
items.rationale: Erosion: the sand is being picked up and removed from where it was.

items.text: Gravity pulls loose rock and soil down a steep slope
items.rationale: Erosion: gravity is moving rock material away from its original spot.

items.text: A river slows as it enters a lake and drops its sand
items.rationale: Deposition: slower water can't carry as much, so the sand settles and builds up in a new place.

items.text: A melting glacier leaves behind a ridge of the rock it carried
items.rationale: Deposition: where the glacier's ice melts, the rock it was carrying is dropped and piles up into a ridge (a moraine) in a new place.

questions.explanation: Ask what is happening to the rock material. If it is breaking down where it sits, whether it cracks apart or a chemical reaction makes it crumble, that is weathering. If it is being picked up and carried off by wind, water, ice or gravity, that is erosion. If carried material is settling and piling up in a new place, that is deposition.
questions.misconception: Weathering, erosion and deposition are three names for the same thing: rock wearing away.
questions.hint: For each change, ask one question: is the rock breaking, moving, or settling?

questions.prompt: After a cold winter, a boulder on a mountainside has split into several chunks, all still sitting where the boulder was. A friend says, "The boulder has eroded." What is the best correction?
questions.accessiblePrompt: After a cold winter, a boulder on a mountainside has split into several chunks, all still sitting where the boulder was. A friend says, "The boulder has eroded." What is the best correction?

choices.text: It weathered: it broke apart, but nothing has carried the pieces off yet
choices.rationale: Correct. Breaking rock where it sits is weathering. Erosion starts only when water, wind, ice or gravity carries the pieces away.

choices.text: Your friend is right: any rock that breaks apart has eroded
choices.rationale: Breaking is weathering, not erosion. Erosion means the pieces are carried away, and these chunks have not moved.

choices.text: It was deposited: the chunks settled into a new place
choices.rationale: Deposition is carried material settling somewhere new. These chunks were never carried anywhere.

choices.text: It weathered and eroded at once, since breaking and moving are one process
choices.rationale: They are separate steps. Weathering can happen without erosion, as it did here.

questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock down; erosion carries the pieces away. The two often happen one after the other, but they are separate steps. Here the boulder has broken, yet every chunk is still in place, so only weathering has happened. If spring meltwater later washes the chunks downhill, that will be erosion.
questions.misconception: Any wearing down of rock counts as erosion, even when nothing has moved.
questions.hint: Reread where the chunks are now. What would erosion have done to them?

questions.prompt: The sand grains in the Namib Desert's dunes were once part of solid rock. Which process turned that solid rock into loose sand grains in the first place?

choices.text: Weathering
choices.rationale: Correct. Over long spans of time, weathering broke solid rock into smaller and smaller pieces until they were sand-sized.

choices.text: Uplift
choices.rationale: Uplift raises large areas of crust. It doesn't make loose grains, and sand isn't pushed up from below.

choices.text: Erosion
choices.rationale: Erosion moves grains from place to place, but the grains had to be broken off rock before they could travel.

questions.explanation: Most sand, including the Namib's, starts as solid rock. questions.hint: Wind and water can carry sand, but where did each grain come from in the first place?

questions.prompt: Most caves form in limestone. What mainly opens up the empty space of a limestone cave over hundreds of thousands of years?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Most caves form in a rock called limestone. What mainly opens up the empty space of a limestone cave over hundreds of thousands of years?

choices.text: Rushing water smashes the rock apart by force
choices.rationale: Moving water can wear rock, but limestone caves open up mainly by dissolving, a chemical change, not by smashing.

choices.text: Underground heat melts the limestone away
choices.rationale: Rock near the surface is nowhere near hot enough to melt. The limestone dissolves instead.

choices.text: Weakly acidic water dissolves the limestone
choices.rationale: Correct. Water carrying a little dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with limestone and carries it away in solution. That is chemical weathering.

choices.text: Earthquakes crack the limestone open into big spaces
choices.rationale: Cracks guide where water seeps in, but the big open spaces come from the limestone dissolving, not from the ground splitting apart.

questions.explanation: Rainwater picks up a little carbon dioxide and becomes a weak acid. As it seeps through cracks, it reacts with the limestone and carries the rock away dissolved. This chemical weathering is very slow: even fast-growing stream passages widen by about 1 millimeter a year at most, so big caves take hundreds of thousands of years.
questions.misconception: Caves are blasted out by the force of moving water or melted out by heat, not dissolved by a chemical reaction.
questions.hint: A cave is a huge space where rock used to be, yet there is usually no giant pile of rubble left behind. Where could all that rock have gone?

questions.prompt: A drill brings up sand from deep beneath newer layers. Their weight has packed the grains tightly, yet the sample still crumbles in your hand. What still has to happen for this sand to become sandstone?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A drill brings up sand from deep underground, beneath newer layers of sediment. The weight of those layers has packed the grains tightly, yet the sample still crumbles in your hand. What still has to happen for this sand to become sandstone?

choices.text: Minerals left by groundwater must glue the grains together
choices.rationale: Correct. Weight packs the grains (compaction), but minerals left between them by groundwater are what bind them into rock (cementation).

choices.text: Far more weight must squeeze the grains until they melt together
choices.rationale: Sandstone forms without melting; melted rock cools into igneous rock instead. More weight packs the grains tighter, but it is mineral cement that binds them.

choices.text: The layer must be lifted back up to Earth's surface
choices.rationale: Uplift can expose sandstone later, but it does not turn loose sand into rock.

choices.text: Wind or water must carry the grains to a new place first
choices.rationale: This sand was already carried and laid down. Moving it again would undo the packing, not finish the rock.

questions.explanation: Turning sand into sandstone takes two overlapping steps. The weight of newer layers squeezes the grains closer together (compaction). Groundwater seeping through the gaps leaves minerals such as calcium carbonate that glue the grains together (cementation). Without that natural cement, even tightly packed sand stays crumbly.
questions.misconception: The weight of overlying layers alone turns sand into solid rock.
questions.hint: Compare this crumbly sand with a solid block of sandstone. Is the difference how tightly the grains are packed, or something else?

questions.accessiblePrompt: Which statement best describes the principle of uniformitarianism, a key idea geologists use to study Earth's history?

choices.text: Earth's surface stays uniform and never really changes
choices.rationale: The name is misleading. The principle is about processes staying the same, while the surface itself changes constantly.

choices.text: Processes at work today also worked in the past
choices.rationale: Correct. The processes we can observe now operated in the past too, so the present helps explain Earth's history.

choices.text: Earth's features were mostly made by a few huge disasters
choices.rationale: That describes an older rival idea. Uniformitarianism explains features mostly with ordinary processes still at work today.

choices.text: Faraway places on Earth tend to have the same kinds of landforms
choices.rationale: Landforms differ a lot from place to place. The principle says the processes follow the same rules, not that landscapes match.

questions.explanation: Uniformitarianism says the natural processes we can observe now, such as gravity pulling rock downhill or rivers dropping sand, also worked in the past and will keep working. That is why geologists say the present is the key to the past. It does not mean Earth never changes; it means the causes of change stay the same.
questions.misconception: Uniformitarianism means Earth's surface is uniform or unchanging.
questions.hint: Don't let the word 'uniform' fool you. The principle is not about Earth looking the same.

left.text: A jumble of sharp, broken rock piled at the foot of a steep slope
left.rationale: Pieces fell or slid down from higher ground: today, loose rock on steep slopes falls or slides downhill and piles up at the bottom, so a heap like this marks rock that gravity brought down.

left.text: Sandstone with tall, sweeping, slanted layers like those inside modern sand dunes
left.rationale: Wind once heaped loose grains into tall hills here: dunes built by wind today have slanted inner layers (cross-bedding), so sandstone with the same pattern records ancient dunes.

left.text: A layer of rounded pebbles, sorted by size, far from any stream today
left.rationale: Flowing water once tumbled this material and dropped it here: flowing water rounds pebbles as it tumbles them and drops them where it slows, so a layer like this marks where water once flowed.

left.text: A sheet of dark volcanic rock covering an old valley floor
left.rationale: Molten rock once poured out here and cooled: eruptions today send lava across the land, where it cools into rock, so a sheet like this records an eruption long ago.

right.text: Pieces fell or slid down from higher ground
Wind once heaped loose grains into tall hills here
Flowing water once tumbled this material and dropped it here
Molten rock once poured out here and cooled

questions.explanation: Each clue is explained by a process we can watch today: gravity piling broken rock below slopes, wind heaping sand into dunes, streams dropping pebbles where they slow, and lava hardening into rock. Because the same kinds of processes worked in the past, today's observations let geologists read a landscape's history.
questions.misconception: We can't know anything about how a landscape formed unless someone watched it happen.
questions.hint: For each clue, ask which process you could watch today that leaves that kind of trace.

questions.prompt: Old photos show a natural stone arch getting a little thinner every decade. A ranger predicts that it will someday collapse. Which reason best supports her prediction?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Old photographs show a natural stone arch getting a little thinner every decade. A park ranger predicts that the arch will someday collapse. Which reason best supports her prediction?

choices.text: The processes that thinned it are still at work and will keep working
choices.rationale: Correct. Processes seen working now can be expected to keep working, so the thinning continues until the arch can't hold itself up.

choices.text: It has stood so long that it is due to fall within days
choices.rationale: Age alone doesn't set a date. The arch falls when wearing has thinned it too much, which could be years or centuries away.

choices.text: The old photos let her calculate the exact year it will fall
choices.rationale: Photos show the direction of change, not a date. Hidden cracks and storms make the timing uncertain.

choices.text: The arch was carved by one huge flood long ago, and floods like that come back
choices.rationale: The photos show the arch wearing slowly, a little each decade, not changing all at once in a single disaster.

questions.explanation: A good prediction rests on processes we can watch working now. Wind, water and gravity thinned the arch, and they will keep thinning it until it can no longer hold itself up. Those processes tell us the direction of change, but not the day it will fall.
questions.misconception: A landform's future can be predicted from its age alone, or timed to an exact date.
questions.hint: Which reason uses something the ranger can actually see happening?
